Foreword

Status: SHIPPED. The event vocabulary predates this spec (the writers own their events, §2.3); this spec owns the READ contract and the anchor: the filter grammar, the output documents, the chain, the named errors — and the walk an auditor with no tebako knowledge follows to prove, offline, what ran on a host.

1. The ledger and its one job

Every tebako process writes one append-only line per decision worth auditing into a single host-local file:

The line shape is shared by both writers — the bootstrap (the loader's fetch / verify / mount / exec decisions) and tfs::journal (the driver's and preload's policy, VFS, overlay and decrypt decisions):

The ledger answers exactly one question — "what ran here, and why did it run?" — for one host, from one file, with no network and no other tebako artifact. It is not aggregated, not sharded, not rotated by the tools (an operator may rotate it; --seal before rotation is the discipline that keeps the seam auditable).

The read-only law. A query (tebako audit … without --seal) creates nothing, appends nothing, stamps nothing, migrates nothing. It runs on a host whose ~/.tebako was written by an older tebako, and it must not move that store's layout forward on the way in. The single writing verb is --seal, and the only file it writes is the anchor (§4).

2. Reading rules (normative)

2.1 Line grammar

  • The first space-delimited token is the timestamp: unix seconds, decimal. 0 is legitimate (a clock failure never fails the audited operation).

  • Every following token is key=value, split at the FIRST =, so a value may itself contain = (URLs with query strings, base64).

  • A token that carries no = CONTINUES the previous value, joined by one space. Writers record paths, and paths contain spaces: a legitimate path=/a b/c must not turn into damage. A leading token without = before any key exists is damage.

  • event= is the required key: a line without it, or with an unreadable timestamp, is malformed (§2.2).

  • A trailing newline terminates the record; a final record without one is still a record (the bytes are the record).

  • Duplicate keys: the FIRST statement stands (§5's fields_map_rule) — a writer's second mention of a key never retroactively rewrites what it already said.

2.2 Damage is surfaced, never swallowed

A line that does not parse is a malformed record: it is counted, carries its 1-based line number, and appears in the JSON document's malformed array with its raw bytes. A ledger that quietly drops what it cannot read is worse than one that admits damage. A query's exit code stays 0 for malformed lines unless --strict is given (§6) — the default posture is "show me everything, including the damage", because an operator diagnosing a host should not have to guess what was hidden.

A malformed line is still a LINE: it occupies its position in the file and it is covered by the anchor's chain exactly like a readable one (a deleted line moves every later record, readable or not). "Record" and "line" are therefore interchangeable in the anchor's vocabulary (§4).

2.3 The vocabulary (by the question it answers)

The writers own their event names — this table is the census, and it exists so an auditor can phrase a filter. It is not exhaustive: an unknown event= value is a first-class record, filterable like any other (forward compatibility is the point of a ledger).

3. The query surface

3.1 Filters

Table 2
flagmeaning
--since <t>keep records with ts >= t. t is unix seconds or RFC 3339 UTC (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ).
--until <t>keep records with ts <= t. Same grammar.
--event <e>[,<e>…]keep records whose event= is one of the listed names. Repeatable; the union of all occurrences. Exact match, never a prefix.
--artifact <needle>keep records whose body (everything after the timestamp) CONTAINS needle — the artifact reference as the writer recorded it: a payload name, a version, a sha256, a URL fragment. Case-sensitive, documented as a substring so nobody mistakes it for a structured field.
--tail <n>after filtering, keep only the last n records.

Filters compose with AND across flags, OR within --event. No filter means the whole ledger. A time filter's grammar is exact: local time is never inferred, because a silently shifted window is a silently wrong answer.

--seal takes NO filters (an anchor covers the whole file or it is not an anchor) and --seal with --verify is refused by name: one writes, the other checks.

3.2 Output

Default (line mode). The matching records, verbatim — the ledger's own bytes, in file order — so a reader can pipe them to sha256sum and compare against a seal. A one-line summary (N of M record(s)) goes to STDERR, never into the stream: the stdout of a query is a ledger excerpt, not a report about one.

--count. Exactly the match count on stdout, nothing else.

--json. The audit_schema: 1 document (§5) on stdout alone; the version banner moves to stderr, like every other machine contract in this toolchain.

File order is preserved in every mode. A ledger's order IS evidence; re-sorting it would destroy the only thing the file cannot be rebuilt without.

4. The anchor: tamper evidence

An append-only file with no anchor proves nothing — anyone can edit a line, or delete a run's records entirely, and the file still looks like a ledger. The anchor is a chained digest, sealed on demand and verified on demand, stored BESIDE the journal it covers and named by it:

Beside, not inside: the journal stays a pure record stream, every reader of it keeps working, and an explicit TEBAKO_JAIL_JOURNAL override carries its seal along instead of splitting the pair across two homes.

4.1 The chain

where ‖ is byte concatenation of the raw 32-byte digest with the line's exact bytes INCLUDING its terminating newline. Any edit, any deletion, any insertion shifts every subsequent digest — the anchor's whole value is that it cannot be recomputed without re-sealing, and a re-seal is itself a new record (§4.3).

The terminator is normalized: a final record whose newline an editor added or stripped is the same ledger. That one cosmetic difference is the only edit the anchor does not report, and it is reported as nothing because it changes nothing an auditor reads.

4.2 Seal records

One line per seal, appended to the seal file:

  • head — the chain digest over the journal's first lines lines.

  • lines — how many lines the seal covers (the file's state at seal time; later lines are the unsealed tail).

  • key / sig — the seal's authenticity. When a signing key is available (the machine's press-local key, spec 09), the canonical payload

    is signed detached (OpenPGP — the one mechanism this project uses) and sig carries the armored signature hex-encoded. With no key, both fields are -.

The unsigned seal is honest about what it is. It detects edits (a changed line no longer hashes to the sealed head) but not forgery (somebody with write access can rewrite the log and re-seal). The verb says so on stderr every time it writes one:

A signed seal, verified against the trusted keyring or a pinned key, is the enterprise answer.

A seal that cannot be produced because the key store refuses is a LOUD unsigned seal, never a failed seal: an unanchorable ledger is worse than an unsigned anchor. A TEBAKO_SIGN that is not a boolean is a named usage error, never a silent choice.

4.3 Verification

  • Recompute the chain over the WHOLE journal and compare it against the seals. The LAST seal speaks for the file; the earlier ones LOCATE the damage.

  • Walking the seals in order: the newest seal whose recomputed chain still matches marks the end of the known-good prefix, and the first seal after it names the interval that changed. That interval — [known_good+1, failing.lines], 1-based and inclusive — is what the report prints, because "records 411–812 changed" is actionable and "the head differs" is not.

  • A seal covering more lines than the file holds is not a prefix mismatch but a REMOVAL: the report says records are gone, and names the same interval.

  • Three outcomes: sealed (the last seal matches), tampered (it does not, or a signed seal's signature does not validate → exit 80), unsealed (no seal file: named, exit 74, with the remedy — "run tebako audit --seal").

  • A signed seal's signature is checked against the trusted keyring and the pinned trust store. An unknown signer is reported as unknown-key and the outcome stays sealed (the chain matched) with the authenticity gap NAMED, never quietly upgraded. An invalid signature is tampered, whatever the chain says — a valid chain under a forged seal is exactly what a re-seal looks like.

  • A seal file with an unparseable line is a finding (exit 80), never a skipped line: corrupting the anchor is an attacker's first move, so damage there is never noise.

5. The JSON contract (audit_schema: 1)

Table 3
fieldmeaning
matched / totalrecords selected by the filters, and lines the file holds
records[].fieldsthe record's k=v tokens as a map, first-wins on duplicate keys
records[].rawthe record's exact bytes without the newline
malformed[]unparseable lines, always present (empty array when clean)
verifynull for a query; the object above for --verify; absent for --seal, whose document carries seal instead
verify.divergence{"from_line": N, "to_line": M} when the outcome is tampered, else null
seal (on --seal){path, ts, head, lines, signer} — signer is null when unsigned

records is capped by --tail and by the filters; total always reports the file, so a filtered document can never be mistaken for the whole ledger. audit_schema is 1 forever: extensions add keys, never retype or rename one.

6. Named errors and exit codes

Table 4
codenamemeaning
80EX_TEBAKO_LEDGER--verify found a mismatch or an invalid seal signature; an unparseable seal record; or --strict with malformed journal lines
74EX_TEBAKO_IOthe journal or seal cannot be read or written; a query on a host with no journal yet; --verify with no seal yet
64EX_USAGEunparseable filter or time, unknown flag, --seal with filters, --seal together with --verify

Every message names the file and the remedy — never "invalid input".

7. The auditor's walk

The arc's acceptance, spelled out as the steps an auditor with no tebako knowledge performs. Each step is offline and needs only public artifacts plus this document:

  1. tebako audit --json > ledger.json — the host's decisions.

  2. tebako audit --event fetch,runtime-fetch-verified --json — every byte source and its verification verdict.

  3. Take any sha256 from step 2 and check the artifact against the registry row and its attestation (gh attestation verify), then reproduce the payload image per spec 14's reproducible-press rule.

  4. tebako audit --verify — the ledger's own integrity, against the seal the host wrote; or tebako audit --seal first on a host that never anchored.

  5. Confirm the mount set (--event composition,overlay,decrypt) matches the package's declared dependency tree (tebako closure).

  6. Archive ledger.json + the seal file; a later --verify on the archived pair proves the archive is what the host wrote.

8. What this spec does not own

  • The event names and their field vocabularies — the writers own those (§2.3 is a census, not a registry).

  • Rotation, retention, remote shipping: operator policy. The seal is the seam that makes rotation auditable, and that is all this spec says about it.

  • The signature mechanism itself: spec 09 owns OpenPGP, the keyring and the pinned trust store; this spec only names where a seal's signature is checked.
